title: NTL amplification in a SuperCDMS-style detector fabricated from a University of South Dakota-grown germanium crystal
authors: Dongming Mei, Gerardo Gonzalez, William Baker, Mark Platt, Nader Mirabolfathi
abstract: Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) amplification enables eV-sub-keV detection thresholds for low-mass dark-matter and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering experiments. We evaluated two University of South Dakota (USD)-grown germanium crystals fabricated as SuperCDMS-style four-channel athermal-phonon detectors and operated near 10 mK. The crystals had electrically active impurity concentrations near $10^10~\mathrm^-3$ and etch-pit densities of $300$-$7000~\mathrm^-2$. Contact-free biasing produced no resolvable amplification. However, after depositing a 600 nm aluminum bias contact, Detector~2 exhibited clear voltage-dependent NTL gain. The reconstructed channel-B energy increased from approximately 3.9 keV at 0 V to 34.9 keV at 40 V, corresponding to an 8.9-fold enhancement. Statistical centroid uncertainties were below 0.3%, while low-bias fits yielded effective prompt- and NTL-phonon response coefficients of $(6.77\pm0.82)%$ and $(4.77\pm0.20)%$, respectively, excluding systematic uncertainties. These results demonstrate the feasibility of USD-grown germanium for SuperCDMS-style high-voltage phonon detectors and highlight the importance of both crystal quality and contact fabrication in achieving NTL amplification.
summary: This experimental paper reports on the successful demonstration of Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) phonon amplification in a SuperCDMS-style detector made from University of South Dakota germanium. By applying a deposited aluminum bias contact, the researchers achieved a significant, voltage-dependent enhancement in the measurable phonon signal. This work validates the use of these specific crystal materials and fabrication techniques for next-generation, low-threshold dark matter and neutrino detectors.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) amplification in SuperCDMS-style cryogenic detectors using germanium crystals grown at the University of South Dakota.
main_result: Contacting the detector with a deposited aluminum bias film enabled clear, voltage-dependent NTL gain, showing an enhancement factor of approximately 8.9 between 0 V and 40 V bias.
method: The experiment involved operating the detector at 10 mK, varying the bias voltage from 0 V to 40 V, and analyzing the resulting phonon signals using superconducting transition-edge sensors (TES).
model_or_system: The physical system is a SuperCDMS-style four-channel athermal-phonon detector fabricated from USD-grown germanium. The underlying physics involves the NTL amplification mechanism, where the total phonon energy is enhanced by the applied bias voltage.
key_observables: Voltage-dependent NTL gain (e.g., energy increasing from 3.9 keV to 34.9 keV), and measured effective prompt- and NTL-phonon response coefficients.
important_parameters: Crystal impurity concentration ($\sim 10^{10} 	ext{ cm}^{-3}$), etch-pit density ($300–7000 	ext{ cm}^{-2}$), and operating temperature ($\sim 10 	ext{ mK}$).
main_assumptions: The measured response coefficients exclude systematic uncertainties related to full calibration or TES response, and the results are considered a 'proof-of-principle' rather than a final qualification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate detector configurations, amplitude spectra showing the lack of gain in contact-free runs, and LPF-amplitude histograms used for quantitative peak extraction across varying bias voltages.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for NTL amplification for low-mass dark matter searches, detailing the experimental setup using USD-Ge crystals, showing the failure of initial contact-free tests, and finally presenting the successful, quantified NTL gain achieved after depositing a continuous aluminum bias contact.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is particle astrophysics detection, the underlying physics involves charge transport and energy deposition in a solid-state semiconductor at cryogenic temperatures, which touches upon concepts relevant to quantum transport and energy dissipation in condensed matter systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Detector configurations used in the test campaign. Detector 2 was 75 mm in diameter, 10 mm thick, and had a mass of 230 g. It carried four phonon channels on the instrumented face. Initial operation used a mechanically separated contact-free electrode. The successful final run used a continuous 600 nm Al electrode deposited on the opposite face with a modified Perkin Elmer 4400 sputter coater. The 1 𝜇Ci 241Am source was positioned above channel B at a source-to-detector distance of 26 mm. Photographs are not to a common scale.

Figure 2. Amplitude spectra from the second detector in the contact-free configuration at 0 V, 5 V, 10 V, and 15 V. No systematic NTL-induced peak displacement was resolved. The absent fourth panel denotes channel C unavailable during this run and must not be interpreted as a zero-response measurement.

Figure 3. One-second waveform segments illustrating the environmental-noise limitation. Compressor operation generated strong microphonic structure; with the compressor off, the baseline became substantially quieter, although narrow-band electrical pickup remained in at least one channel.

Figure 4. Final-run low-pass-filter (LPF) amplitude spectra for channels B (left) and C (right) at 0 V, 5 V, 10 V, 15 V, 20 V, 30 V and 40 V. The curves overlaid on the channel-B histograms are the Gaussian fits used to obtain the quantitative peak positions reported in Table 3. The optimal filter was used only to estimate pulse timing and thereby provide an approximate search location for LPF amplitude extraction. Channel B shows clear voltage-dependent NTL amplification. The weak response in channel C is consistent with the 241Am source placement over channel B and local phonon collection.

Figure 4 shows the final LPF-amplitude spectra from channels B and C and the Gaussian curves used in the quantitative peak extraction. The channel-B centroid values and statistical uncertainties listed in Table 3 are obtained from these LPF-amplitude distributions; the optimal filter was used only for pulse timing, as described in Sec. 2.5. Channel B exhibits a sequence of well-separated spectral maxima that move to larger pulse amplitude as the bias increases from 0 V to 40 V. The Gaussian centroid increases from (2.377 ± 0.006) 𝜇A at 0 V to (16.420 ± 0.029) 𝜇A at 40 V.
